title: If Christ be not risen (1 Corinthians 15:14; CCC 639)
hook: Catholics hold the resurrection happened, not as a metaphor

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Paschal mystery: the cross and the rising as one passage. Your line was through death to life. Today, the second half of that passage, and one very blunt sentence.

Word reaches the man who founded the church in Corinth: some members are saying the dead don't really rise. He could soften it. Say the story is beautiful, whatever happened. Say what matters is what Jesus taught. Instead he writes one of the bluntest sentences you could put in a letter: if it didn't happen, our preaching is empty, and so is your faith. He bets everything on one event. The writer is Paul, the letter is First Corinthians, and the Catholic Church still stands behind his bet.
screen: `SOME SAY THE DEAD DON'T RISE.` → `HE DOESN'T SOFTEN IT.` → `HE BETS EVERYTHING ON ONE EVENT.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "And if Christ be not risen again, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain." Vain means empty. Paul goes further: if Christ isn't raised, Christians are still in their sins, and if their hope is for this life only, they are of all people the most miserable. Then the witnesses. Just before this, Paul lists who saw the risen Jesus: Cephas, that's Peter, then the apostles, then more than five hundred people at once, many of whom, he says, are still alive. That detail reads like an invitation: go and ask them. And Paul says he is handing on what he himself received, so the list was already being passed along before he wrote it down. The Catechism calls the resurrection a real event, with manifestations that were historically witnessed, as the New Testament shows. Not a metaphor for the disciples' hope, not a way of saying his teaching lived on. The tomb was empty, and he was seen. And the Catechism points out that the disciples were not easy believers: they thought the women's report was nonsense, and Thomas refused to believe unless he could touch the wounds. What kind of rising? Not a return to the old life, the way Lazarus came back and would later die again. Catholics say Jesus rose into a glorified life that death can't touch: still bearing the wounds, able to eat with friends, no longer bound by locked doors. And in Matthew, the angel at the empty tomb answers Paul's if in three words: he is risen.
screen: `IF NOT, OUR FAITH IS VAIN.` · `MORE THAN FIVE HUNDRED AT ONCE.` · `A REAL EVENT, NOT A METAPHOR.` · `NOT LAZARUS: A GLORIFIED LIFE.` · then, large: `HE IS RISEN.`

segments.voice: Picture the early morning: the stone rolled back, the women running, Peter running after them. Then say the three words quietly, he is risen, and again, slower, and notice what comes, joy, doubt or both, and let it be honest; Thomas had doubt, and he's a saint. If you pray, you can bring the doubt and the joy to God together.
Egerthe, the Greek word the angel uses at the empty tomb: he was raised, he is risen. Paul's whole bet on one event.
Your line: he is risen. Not a metaphor: Catholics hold that it happened. Day three hundred six, done.

howItsDone: Catholics profess every Sunday in the Creed that Christ rose on the third day, celebrate the resurrection for the fifty days of Easter, and in many communities, especially Eastern Catholic ones, greet each other at Easter with Christ is risen, and the reply, he is truly risen.

trapdoor: what you thought: Easter is a story about hope.
what it means: Catholics hold that Jesus truly rose, bodily and glorified, and that the faith stands or falls on it.
what a scholar hears: 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 as an early received formula; Paul's 'I received' (15:3); egerthe; the empty tomb and the appearances.

sources.quoted: And if Christ be not risen again, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain.

notes: Douay-Rheims 1 Corinthians 15:14 given from memory; confirm.
Dating of 1 Corinthians to the mid-50s and 15:3–8 as a pre-Pauline formula: mainstream scholarship; confirm framing.
CCC 639, 643, 646 paraphrased (real event; disciples not credulous; not a return to earthly life). Confirm.
Greek ἠγέρθη (Matthew 28:6; Mark 16:6) given for 'he is risen'; confirm accent and transliteration.
Paschal greeting is most associated with Eastern Catholic and Orthodox communities; now only in howItsDone.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'Imagine' and drops the unsourced 'twenty-some years'; 'the twelve' changed to 'the apostles' (Douay-Rheims 1 Cor 15:5 reads 'the eleven', the Greek 'the twelve'); 'most of whom are still alive' corrected to 'many' (Douay-Rheims 15:6: 'many remain'); mid-50s date and 'many scholars think' cut, replaced with Paul's own 'which I also received' (15:3); Thomas 'refused to believe unless he could touch' (John 20:25 never says he touched); closing 'he is risen' now tied to the angel in Matthew 28:6, not to an Easter greeting that actually says 'Christ is risen'.
